name: Ahimaaz
title: Son of Zadok – Runner and Messenger for King David
summary: Ahimaaz, son of the high priest Zadok, played a crucial role during Absalom's rebellion against King David. Together with Jonathan, son of Abiathar, he was stationed at the spring En-Rogel outside Jerusalem, where the two served as courageous intelligence couriers who relayed vital messages from David's counselor Hushai to the fleeing king. When they were discovered by Absalom's men, a woman in Bahurim saved them by hiding them in a well and misleading their pursuers. Ahimaaz was also known for his exceptional speed as a runner. After the decisive battle where Absalom fell, he insisted on bringing the news to David, chose an alternative route through the Jordan Valley, and passed the first messenger, Cushite. His conduct when he reached the king demonstrated both courage and wisdom: he delivered the message of victory but tactfully refrained from telling David directly about his son's death, leaving that heavy news to the Cushite. A person with the same name is later mentioned as one of King Solomon's twelve district governors responsible for Naphtali, married to the king's daughter Basemath—an identification that is plausible but uncertain.

keyEvents.title: Stationed as an intelligence courier at En-Rogel
keyEvents.description: Ahimaaz and Jonathan, the son of Abiathar, were stationed at En-Rogel to receive intelligence from Hushai and bring it to David during Absalom's rebellion.

keyEvents.title: Hidden in the well at Bahurim
keyEvents.description: When Absalom's servants hunted Ahimaaz and Jonathan, a woman in Bahurim hid them in a well, covered it over, and misled their pursuers.

keyEvents.title: Delivered Hushai's advice to David
keyEvents.description: After escaping their pursuers, Ahimaaz and Jonathan ran to David and conveyed the crucial counsel that he must cross the Jordan immediately, based on Hushai's intelligence regarding Ahithophel's battle plan.

keyEvents.title: Ran as a messenger after the battle against Absalom
keyEvents.description: After Absalom was killed by Joab, Ahimaaz asked permission to run with the message to David. Joab first sent the Cushite, but Ahimaaz insisted and finally received approval. He took another route through the Jordan Valley and arrived first.

keyEvents.title: Brought the victory report to David
keyEvents.description: Ahimaaz reached David before the Cushite and reported the victory, but avoided telling him directly about Absalom's death. When David asked if Absalom was safe, Ahimaaz evasively replied that he had seen a great commotion but did not know what it meant. In this way, he spared the grieving father's heart—at least for a moment.

keyEvents.title: Possible district governor under Solomon
keyEvents.description: An Ahimaaz is mentioned as one of Solomon's twelve district governors, married to Solomon's daughter Basemath, with responsibility for the Naphtali region. Identifying him as Zadok's son is plausible but not certain.

versions.summary: Ahimaaz was the son of the high priest Zadok and served as a key messenger for King David during Absalom's rebellion. He was known for his speed as a runner and his loyalty to David. He played a crucial role in conveying intelligence from Jerusalem to David while the king was fleeing.
versions.title: Zadok's son and messenger
versions.reason: [major] The roles 'leader' and 'warrior' are imprecise for Ahimaaz. He was primarily a messenger/runner and spy, not a warrior or leader in the traditional sense. He was also a priest's son and possibly an official under Solomon.; [minor] The description says "This is often identified with Zadok's son," which is somewhat vague. It could be formulated more precisely to reflect the academic uncertainty.; [minor] If Ahimaaz in 1 Kings 4:15 is identified as Zadok's son, he was married to Basemath, Solomon's daughter. This should be considered for inclusion, possibly with a footnote noting the uncertainty.; [minor] Footnotes are completely missing. There are interesting linguistic, historical, and theological aspects concerning Ahimaaz that should be covered.

versions.summary: Ahimaaz was the son of the high priest Zadok and served as an important messenger and intelligence agent for King David during Absalom's rebellion. He was known for his speed as a runner and his loyalty to David. Together with Jonathan, the son of Abiathar, he played a crucial role in conveying strategically vital intelligence from Jerusalem to David while the king was fleeing. After the victory over Absalom, he ran with the message to David but tactfully avoided telling him directly about Absalom's death. He is possibly also mentioned as one of Solomon's governors in Naphtali.

versions.reason: [minor] The role of 'spy' can be somewhat misleading. Ahimaaz functioned more as an intelligence courier than a spy in the traditional sense. He did not gather information himself but received and relayed it. 'Intelligence courier' or 'runner' would have been more precise. 'Runner' is also an important role that should be mentioned explicitly, since his speed is a prominent feature in the text.; [minor] The summary is good and informative, but this is now the second version and should clearly differentiate itself from version 1. The wording is already quite similar. It could be improved with more theological reflection on his character and role in the narrative tension of 2 Samuel.; [minor] The footnote about Talmud Sanhedrin 95b: This reference primarily concerns David and the risk he exposed himself to in war, not directly the messenger's role in bringing bad news. It is better to refer more generally to rabbinic tradition regarding the delivery of bad news, or to adjust the reference.; [minor] According to 1 Kings 4:15, Ahimaaz may have been married to Basemath, Solomon's daughter. Although the identification is uncertain (as correctly noted in keyEvents), this could be mentioned as a possible spouse with appropriate caution, for the sake of completeness.

versions.summary: Ahimaaz, son of the high priest Zadok, played a key role in the drama surrounding Absalom's rebellion against King David. Stationed at En-Rogel together with Jonathan, son of Abiathar, he served as a courageous intelligence courier who brought vital messages from Hushai in Jerusalem to the fleeing king. When the two were discovered by Absalom's men, they were saved by being hidden in a well in Bahurim. Ahimaaz was especially known for his speed as a runner – after the decisive battle where Absalom fell, he insisted on bringing the news of victory to David and ran past the first messenger, the Cushite. His tactful handling of the situation upon arrival, where he refrained from telling David directly about Absalom's death, testifies to a man with both physical strength and emotional wisdom. He is possibly also mentioned as one of Solomon's twelve governors responsible for the Naphtali district, married to the king's daughter Basemath.
versions.title: Son of Zadok – Runner and Messenger for King David
versions.reason: [minor] The summary mentions that Ahimaaz may have been married to Solomon's daughter Basemath (1 Kings 4:15). Although the identification is uncertain, the spouse field could reflect this with a conditional comment, or at least note 'Basemath' as a possible wife for consistency with the rest of the profile.; [minor] The summary is very good and detailed, but the last sentence about Solomon's governor could be strengthened slightly by emphasizing more clearly that this is a tentative identification, distinct from the secure biography. Otherwise, the text is well-phrased and theologically correct.; [minor] 2 Samuel 15:27-29 deals primarily with Zadok and Abiathar being sent back to Jerusalem with their sons. Verses 27-29 mention Zadok and the ark, not directly Ahimaaz's stationing at En-Rogel. Verse 36 mentions Ahimaaz and Jonathan explicitly. Consider limiting the reference to verse 36 in chapter 15, possibly verse 27 as context.

footnotes.text: The name Ahimaaz (Hebrew: אֲחִימַעַץ, Achimaʿats) is composed of אָח (ach, 'brother') and מַעַץ (maʿats), which can mean 'anger' or 'strength'. The name can thus be interpreted as 'my brother is anger' or 'brother to the strong'. The exact meaning of the name is debated among scholars.

En-Rogel, where Ahimaaz and Jonathan were stationed, was a well-known spring southeast of Jerusalem at the confluence of the Hinnom and Kidron valleys. The site has been identified archaeologically and was strategically located outside the city walls, making it an ideal meeting point for secret communication without arousing suspicion.

Ahimaaz's role as a runner reflects an important function in the ancient Near East. Before organized postal systems existed, swift runners served as the primary means of communication in war and politics. Similar systems are known from Egyptian and Mesopotamian sources, and already in David's time such runners were crucial for military intelligence.

The identification of Ahimaaz in 1 Kings 4:15 as the same person as Zadok's son is debated. Some scholars believe it may refer to a different person with the same name, while others see it as a natural career progression from messenger under David to official under Solomon. The time gap between the events is consistent with them being the same person.

Ahimaaz's evasive answer to David about Absalom's fate (2 Sam 18:29) has been the subject of rabbinic discussion. Some rabbis view it as tactful restraint and wisdom—he understood that a father should not hear of his son's death from the first messenger. Others interpret it as him actually not knowing the details. The Midrash tradition reflects on the moral responsibility that comes with bringing bad news to a powerful ruler.

Bahurim, where Ahimaaz and Jonathan were hidden in a well, was a village on the eastern side of the Mount of Olives near Jerusalem. The place is also known from the story of Shimei who cursed David (2 Sam 16:5). The hiding place in the well recalls similar stories in Joshua and Judges about spies being concealed by local helpers.

Ahimaaz's choice of route via the Jordan plain (Hebrew: כִּכָּר, kikkar) instead of the more direct road has sparked interest among geographically oriented biblical scholars. The Jordan plain was flatter and easier to run on, even though it was longer. This shows tactical understanding on Ahimaaz's part—he compensated for the longer distance with better terrain and a faster pace.
